claims.text: For adolescents who perceive low friendship quality, Internet use for communication purposes predicts less depression.
For adolescents who perceive low friendship quality, Internet use for non-communication purposes predicts more depression.
For adolescents who perceive low friendship quality, Internet use for non-communication purposes predicts more social anxiety.
Instant messaging supports social compensation effects on depression for adolescents with low perceived friendship quality.
Non-communication Internet surfing supports poor-get-poorer effects on depression and social anxiety for adolescents with low perceived friendship quality.

evidence.description: Longitudinal questionnaire data gathered from 307 Dutch middle adolescents across two waves with a one-year interval showed communication Internet use predicted less depression among those perceiving low friendship quality.

Two-wave longitudinal questionnaire data from 307 Dutch middle adolescents showed non-communication Internet use predicted higher depression scores in adolescents with low perceived friendship quality.
Two-wave longitudinal questionnaire data from 307 Dutch middle adolescents showed non-communication Internet use predicted higher social anxiety in adolescents with low perceived friendship quality.
Empirical reduction in depression via communication-based Internet use specifically among low friendship quality adolescents supports the social compensation hypothesis.
Empirical increase in depression and social anxiety via non-communication Internet use specifically among low friendship quality adolescents supports the poor-get-poorer hypothesis.

methodologies.name: Two-wave longitudinal questionnaire study
methodologies.description: A two-wave longitudinal survey design with a one-year interval evaluating different types of Internet use, depression, social anxiety, and perceived friendship quality.
datasets: Questionnaire data from 307 Dutch middle adolescents
